title: The World Born From an Offering
hook: in the Purusha Sukta the world comes from an offering. it's why hindus offer food to god before they eat it
carry: offer it first: the world began as giving
tomorrow: does the Rig Veda rank people by birth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, God is in all this, every face included, and the proportion: all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.

What would you make a world out of? Clay, shaped by a potter's hands, is one answer. A spoken word is another. A seed, a shell, a cosmic egg: people have told it more than one way. The Purusha Sukta's answer comes from the fire ritual the hymn itself describes, where offerings are poured into a flame. In this hymn the world comes from an offering, and the ingredients aren't butter and wood. They're spring, summer and autumn.
screen: `CLAY? A WORD? A SEED?` → `THE HYMN'S ANSWER: AN OFFERING.` → `THE INGREDIENTS ARE SEASONS.`

segments.voice: The word is yajna, an offering poured into fire in Vedic worship. Verse six says that when the gods performed a yajna with the Purusha as the offering, spring was its melted butter, summer its fuel, autumn the offering itself. The year itself, poured into the flame. Verse seven: on the sacred grass they sprinkled him, the one born in the beginning. From that offering, fully given, came the creatures of the air, the forest and the village. Verse nine: from it were born the verses and the chants, the meters and formulas, the Vedas themselves. A hymn telling where hymns come from. So in this telling the world isn't built from outside like a house. It comes from something given. And here's what Hindus do because of it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says beings were created together with yajna, and that the good who eat what remains of the offering are freed from fault, while those who cook only for themselves eat wrong. So Hindus offer first: ghee poured into the havan fire, a plate set before the murti, and only then is it eaten, as prasad, the gift that comes back. Many families say a line from the Gita before meals for the same reason. If the world began as giving, then eating is joining in, not just taking.
screen: `YAJNA: AN OFFERING INTO FIRE.` · `SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN: THE INGREDIENTS.` · `FROM IT: CREATURES, CHANTS AND VERSES.` · `OFFER FIRST. THEN PRASAD.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, or with a glass of water now, pause before the first taste. Hold it, and give it first: silently offer it to God, or if you don't pray, to everyone and everything that brought it to you, the rain, the farmer, the cook. Then eat or drink it slowly, as something given back to you.
The Purusha Sukta. In its middle verses, the gods offer the Purusha, with spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it come creatures, chants and verses.
Your line: offer it first, the world began as giving. In this hymn, even the chants are born from an offering. See you tomorrow.
